title: Last 30 Days Before MDCAT: A Study Plan
excerpt: Your final month before MDCAT isn't the time for new topics — it's the time to convert what you already know into a consistent, exam-ready score. Here's how to structure it.

content.text: The last month has a different job than the rest of your prep

Everything before the final 30 days was about building knowledge. The final 30 days are about something different: converting that knowledge into a score you can actually produce under real exam conditions, reliably, across a full 3-hour paper. Those are related goals, but they're not the same goal — and treating the last month like "more of the same" studying is one of the most common ways students underuse this stretch of time.

If you find yourself starting a topic you've never touched before with less than two weeks to go, that's usually a sign to reconsider — is it truly high-yield enough to justify displacing revision time on material you've already covered? For most students, the honest answer is no.
Shift the ratio from learning to practicing

Early in your prep, most of your time was probably reading, watching lectures, and taking first-pass notes. In the final month, that ratio needs to flip. The bulk of your remaining time should go toward solving MCQs, taking timed mock tests, and reviewing your mistakes — not rereading chapters you've already been through once or twice.

This isn't about abandoning content review entirely. It's about recognizing that at this stage, the highest-value activity is usually testing yourself under conditions that resemble the real exam, then using what that reveals to direct your remaining revision — rather than passively re-reading material and hoping it sticks.
A rough week-by-week shape
There's no single correct plan, since it depends on how far along your prep already is, but a reasonable shape for the last 30 days looks something like this:

Weeks 1–2: Full-syllabus revision pass, weighted by subject. Move through every subject once more, spending time roughly in proportion to how much each one is worth on the actual paper — meaning Biology and Chemistry get the most attention, Physics a solid share, and English and Logical Reasoning smaller but real time slots, not zero. This is also when you should be doing your heaviest MCQ practice, chapter by chapter, to catch gaps while there's still time to fix them.

Week 3: Full-length timed mock tests, done properly. Start taking complete, timed mock papers that mimic the real exam's length and format — not just subject-wise question sets. Treat each one seriously: same time of day as your actual exam if possible, no interruptions, and full review afterward, not just a score glance.

Week 4: Light revision only, error-log focused. In the final stretch, avoid diving into anything you haven't already covered. Focus on reviewing an error log you've been keeping — the specific questions and concepts you've gotten wrong across your mock tests and practice — rather than starting fresh material. This is also when sleep, routine, and reducing new stressors matter more than squeezing in extra hours.

Adjust this shape to where you actually are, not where you wish you were. If your syllabus coverage isn't complete going into the last month, be honest about that early and prioritize accordingly — don't discover the gap in week 4.
Why full-length mocks matter more than they seem to

A lot of students under-invest in full-length, timed practice because subject-wise MCQ sets feel more efficient — you can drill a specific weak chapter directly. But MDCAT isn't a collection of isolated chapter tests; it's a single 3-hour paper where fatigue, pacing across sections, and time pressure all interact. A student who knows the content well but hasn't practiced sustaining focus and pace across a full mock can still underperform relative to their actual knowledge, simply because test day is the first time they're doing all of it at once.

Doing several full-length mocks in the final weeks — not fifteen, but a handful done seriously and reviewed thoroughly — tends to matter more for your actual score than an equivalent number of hours spent only on chapter-wise drilling.
Keep an error log and actually use it

Throughout your mock tests and practice sets, keep a running log of what you get wrong — not just the topic, but the specific reason: a concept gap, a careless reading error, running out of time, or a genuine content gap. In the final week especially, reviewing this log is often more valuable than any other single activity, because it's a direct map of where your remaining marks are hiding.
Protect your sleep and routine in the final week

It's tempting to trade sleep for extra study hours as the exam approaches, but this tends to backfire — MDCAT tests sustained concentration and processing speed over three hours, both of which suffer noticeably with poor sleep. In the final week especially, a well-rested, focused few hours of review generally outperforms a sleep-deprived cram session covering more ground but retained less of it.
A simple checklist for the last 30 days

items: Shift your time ratio from learning new content to active MCQ and mock-test practice
Complete one more full pass through the syllabus, weighted toward Biology and Chemistry
Take several full-length, timed mock tests in the middle stretch, and review each one properly
Maintain and revisit an error log throughout
Reserve the final week for light revision and rest, not new material
Prioritize sleep and a stable routine over squeezing in extra hours at the cost of both

content.text: The bottom line

The last 30 days aren't about cramming in everything you didn't get to earlier — they're about making sure what you already know is genuinely exam-ready. Shift your time toward timed practice, use full-length mocks to build real exam stamina, keep an honest error log, and protect your sleep in the final stretch. A calm, well-rested student who has practiced under real conditions consistently outperforms an exhausted one who tried to learn everything at once in the final weeks.

items.question: Should I start new topics in the last 30 days before MDCAT?
items.answer: Generally no. If you're considering a topic you've never touched with less than two weeks to go, it's rarely high-yield enough to justify displacing revision time on material you've already covered.

items.question: How should my study time shift in the final month?

items.answer: A handful done seriously and reviewed thoroughly — not fifteen. Full-length mocks that mimic the real exam's length and format tend to matter more for your score than an equivalent number of hours spent only on chapter-wise drilling.

items.question: What should I focus on in the final week before MDCAT?
items.answer: Light revision only, focused on your error log — the specific questions and concepts you've gotten wrong across mocks and practice. Avoid starting anything new, and prioritize sleep and a stable routine over extra study hours.

items.question: Is it worth sacrificing sleep for extra study time before the exam?
items.answer: No — MDCAT tests sustained concentration and processing speed over three hours, both of which suffer with poor sleep. A well-rested, focused review session generally outperforms a sleep-deprived cram session that covers more but retains less.
